index_intro: In Massachusetts, when the House and Senate pass different versions of a bill, six legislators negotiate the final text in a conference committee. It's the last point where a bill can still change, and it's normally an opaque process. This is the group of legislators determining the fate of these future laws.
explorer_empty: Select a committee, map area, or toggle to highlight specific legislators.
mine_none: Your legislators are not serving on these conference committees.

hero.lead: When the House and Senate pass different versions of a bill, six legislators work out one final text in a conference committee. Learn how it works, see who’s negotiating and what’s still unresolved, and share your input while they’re still deciding.

steps.p: Each chamber passes a bill and must end up with identical text to pass. If they don't, a conference committee is appointed to reconcile them.
Each chamber names three legislators, including one from the minority party. Together, these six negotiate the final text.
The first meeting is public. The rest are as well, unless a majority votes to close them. A final bill only proceeds once 2/3 of the conferees from each chamber agree.
Once it goes up on the legislature's website, the legislators have at least 24 hours to read it before either chamber can vote.
Each chamber votes without amendments. If either rejects it, the bill can return to a new conference committee, or otherwise it doesn't pass.

hero.sources: From MAPLE’s <1>guide to the legislative process</1> and the legislature’s <3>Joint Rules</3>.
